extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners and PTAB decision-makers (IPR litigators, counsel for petitioners and patent owners, APJs)
extracted.subtask_description: Preparing or evaluating a Patent Owner brief arguing that the PTAB should exercise its discretion to deny institution of an inter partes review under Fintiv and the Director’s memorandum. Focuses on the six Fintiv factors and the additional Director-considered factors for discretionary denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 1: Petitioner intent to seek stays
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner has not indicated that it intends to file for any pre-institution or post-institution stays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If there is no evidence the petitioner will seek a stay (pre- or post-institution) in the parallel district court proceeding, Factor 1 weighs in favor of denying institution. Lack of indication that a stay would be sought or granted supports denial because it increases the likelihood of duplicative proceedings. Example: Patent Owner argues Petitioner made no pre-institution stay request and did not indicate plans for a post-institution stay, so Factor 1 favors denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 2: Proximity of district court trial to PTAB final decision
rubrics_metrics.description: Trial in the district court is estimated to occur approximately one month before the Board’s deadline for a final written decision.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board considers whether the district court trial is scheduled close in time to the PTAB's projected final written decision (including potential extensions per 37 C.F.R. § 42.100(c)). Evidence such as median time-to-trial statistics for the relevant district (e.g., CDCA median time-to-trial) may be considered. Short gaps (one to a few months) between trial and the PTAB’s final decision have been held to favor discretionary denial to avoid inefficiency and duplicative burden. Cite precedents (e.g., Shenzen Tuozhu, EClinicalWorks, Samsung/SiOnyx, Fintiv II) showing similar time gaps weighed in favor of denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 3: Substantial investment in parallel proceeding and petitioner delay
rubrics_metrics.description: The court and the parties have substantially invested in the parallel proceeding, and Petitioner delayed in filing the Petition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor 3 looks to the amount and type of work already completed in the district court (e.g., substantive orders, infringement/invalidity contentions, document production, written discovery, Markman hearing and likely claim construction). If such work is substantially underway or complete at the time of the institution decision, and the petitioner delayed filing the petition (especially after notice of the patent), this factor weighs in favor of denial. Prior decisions denying institution where discovery and Markman were underway are relevant. Demonstrate delay (e.g., petition filed months after complaint or after long knowledge of the patent family).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 4: Substantial overlap of issues and weight of Sotera stipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: The petition and the parallel proceeding raise substantially overlapping issues, and Petitioner’s stipulation fails to quell concerns of inefficiency and inconsistent rulings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether the same claims are challenged in both proceedings and whether the petition uses the same or substantially the same grounds, arguments, and evidence (including the same prior art). Substantial overlap favors denial. Consider the content and breadth of any Sotera stipulation: a narrow stipulation that only waives specific grounds or limits itself to "grounds that could reasonably have been raised" may be given little weight if petitioner reserves rights to assert product/system (unpublished) art or combinations not specifically disclaimed. Cite examples where overlapping claims/prior art and limited stipulations led to denial (e.g., Code200, Motorola/Stewart).

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 5: Whether petitioner is the parallel proceeding defendant
rubrics_metrics.description: Petitioner is the parallel proceeding defendant.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the petitioner is the defendant in district court litigation, this factor generally weighs in favor of discretionary denial. The Board has recognized that a petitioner-defendant relationship supports denying institution where other factors also weigh in favor.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fintiv Factor 6: Whether petition grounds render claims unpatentable (merits)
rubrics_metrics.description: None of the grounds asserted by Petitioner render the claims unpatentable because they do not articulate the core limitations of the claims.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factor 6 assesses the strength of the unpatentability challenge as expressed in the petition’s grounds — do the references and arguments actually teach the core claim limitations? Examples of failures: references that only show "relative movement" but not the claimed "sliding," fixation members that prevent sliding, or energy-absorbing structures that deform rather than permit the claimed sliding. Show how each asserted ground maps (or fails to map) to claim elements; where grounds do not articulate core limitations, Factor 6 favors denial. Use claim language citations and reference excerpts to show gaps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Holistic balancing of efficiency, fairness, and merits (Fintiv overarching principle)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board takes a holistic view of whether efficiency and integrity of the system are best served by denying or instituting review, balancing efficiency, fairness, and the merits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fintiv I requires the Board to weigh all six factors together to determine whether an IPR would be an effective and efficient alternative to district court litigation. Use the six-factor analysis collectively to argue that efficiency, fairness, and merits support exercising discretion to deny. Cite Fintiv I at 5-6 for the holistic balancing standard.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s factor: Strength of the unpatentability challenge
rubrics_metrics.description: The Strength of the Unpatentability Challenge is a separate Director-considered factor; a weak petition (not showing a reasonable likelihood of prevailing) supports discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: While overlapping with Fintiv Factor 6, the Director’s memorandum explicitly lists the strength of the challenge as a standalone consideration. Show why the petition is weak (e.g., gaps in references, reliance on conclusory assertions). Cite Director Stewart’s March 26, 2025 memorandum and prior denials where weak merits led to discretionary denial (e.g., Xerox v. Bytemark discussion of weak expert support).

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s factor: Extent of reliance on expert testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: The extent of the petition’s reliance on expert testimony is a relevant consideration for discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board looks for 'focused expert testimony' — extensive reliance on long, duplicative expert declarations that merely repeat attorney arguments is given little weight and favors discretionary denial. Examples: large expert declarations that paraphrase the petition verbatim (e.g., a 239‑page declaration cited hundreds of times) are problematic. Cite FAQs for Interim Processes No. 22 and Xerox/Bytemark precedent where duplicative expert testimony was accorded little weight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s factor: Settled expectations of the parties (length of time claims in force)
rubrics_metrics.description: Settled expectations of the parties, such as the length of time the claims have been in force, are relevant to discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long periods during which claims were in force and relied upon (e.g., years of maintenance fees paid, patents/licensing, prior public notice) weigh in favor of denial. Show petitioner’s prior knowledge (e.g., publications, IDS, related patent family) and long delay in challenging the patent despite notice. Cite precedents (e.g., iRhythm) where settled expectations supported denial.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s factor: Compelling economic interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Compelling economic interests (Patent Owner’s investment and reliance on the patent for licensing/sales) may support discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Document Patent Owner’s investments (capital contributions, loans, R&D, business development) to demonstrate substantial economic reliance on the patents. Where the Owner has dedicated resources over many years, the Board may weigh maintaining those expectations in favor of denial to permit recouping investment. Provide factual exhibits demonstrating expenditures and business reliance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Director’s factor: Compelling public health interests
rubrics_metrics.description: Compelling public health interests (public-benefit technologies whose continued development is important) may support discretionary denial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the patented technology materially advances public health or safety (e.g., helmet designs reducing traumatic brain injury), show inventor background, research credentials, and how the patented technology benefits public health. The Board may consider promoting continued investment in such technologies when exercising discretion. Provide citations to specification passages and biographical/exhibits showing public-health impact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weight and content of a Sotera stipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: A Sotera stipulation is considered as part of the holistic analysis but is not dispositive; the breadth of the stipulation controls its weight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A robust Sotera stipulation (e.g., disavowing assertion of specific products/systems or certain broader categories in district court) may mitigate overlap concerns, but a narrow stipulation that only waives the specific grounds in the petition or "other grounds that could reasonably have been raised" and otherwise reserves rights to assert product/system art will be given little weight. Show how the petitioner’s stipulation reads and whether it leaves room to assert combinations or product art that would undercut the PTAB proceeding being a true alternative.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of district-court case docket evidence (orders, contentions, discovery, Markman) as factors
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board may consider district court filings and activities (infringement/invalidity contentions, items offered for sale, discovery status, scheduling order, and Markman hearing) when evaluating Fintiv factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide specific docket documents (scheduling orders, invalidity contentions identifying items offered for sale, dates of Markman hearing, document production status) to demonstrate the extent of parallel proceeding investment and overlap. Examples in the brief: reliance on Defendant’s Initial Invalidity Contentions, scheduling order, and list of products offered for sale to show overlapping prior art and substantial court investment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administrative compliance with Interim Director Discretionary Process procedures
rubrics_metrics.description: Comply with procedural requirements of the Interim Director Discretionary Process (e.g., page limits and certification under 37 C.F.R. § 42.24(d) / interim process rules).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow the interim process rules for discretionary denial briefing, including page limits (the brief certified it totals 20 pages as allowed under the Interim Director Discretionary Process) and required certifications. Noncompliance can be raised defensively; include a formal certification of page count and cite the applicable interim process link or authority.
